common_name: Creme Brulee Coreopsis (Pale Butter-Yellow Big Bang Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Creme Brulee is a Big Bang series hybrid and does not come true from seed.

directions: Creme Brulee is one of the softer-toned members of the Big Bang breeding line, opening large, buttery pale-yellow flowers over a dense, mounded clump of narrow foliage. Grow it in lean to average, well-drained soil; overly rich soil or too much shade leads to floppy stems and fewer blooms. It flowers from early summer well into fall and holds up better in heat and humidity than many older tickseed cultivars, drawing bees and small butterflies throughout the season. Shear plants back by roughly a third after the first bloom flush to prompt fresh growth and a second wave of flowers, and lift and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Cambridge Scarlet Bee Balm (Classic Brilliant Red Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; give Cambridge Scarlet good air circulation, since it is more prone to powdery mildew than newer resistant selections.

directions: One of the oldest and most widely grown bee balm selections, Cambridge Scarlet carries dense, shaggy heads of vivid true-scarlet flowers on upright stems above aromatic, mint-family foliage, and remains a benchmark color for red bee balm decades after its introduction. It is a magnet for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees through mid- and late summer, and the crushed leaves release a strong, pleasant bergamot scent. Because it predates the modern mildew-resistant breeding lines, foliage can develop powdery mildew by late summer in humid or crowded conditions, so allow generous spacing and divide the spreading clump every two to three years in spring to keep it open and vigorous. Deadhead to tidy the plant or leave seed heads for finches over winter.

common_name: Blue Stocking Bee Balm (Violet-Purple Bergamot, Blaustrumpf)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space generously for airflow to help limit powdery mildew.

directions: Also sold under its original German name Blaustrumpf, Blue Stocking bears large, tousled flower heads in a rich violet-purple that reads as one of the true 'blue' tones available in bee balm, carried on sturdy stems that need little staking. Bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies visit steadily from midsummer into early fall, and the aromatic foliage keeps its scent well when cut and dried. It shows somewhat better mildew tolerance than older red cultivars but still benefits from full sun, even moisture, and open spacing during humid summers. Divide the spreading clump every two to three years in early spring to renew vigor and keep the colony from crowding itself out.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun; dark stem and foliage color develop best with full sun exposure.

directions: Storm Cloud stands out among blue star cultivars for its near-black stems and dark-tinted new foliage, which contrast strikingly with clusters of soft powder-blue, star-shaped spring flowers before the leaves mature to a more typical green. Like other Amsonia, it forms a dense, shrub-like clump that needs no staking, shrugs off summer heat and drought once established, and turns a glowing gold in autumn. It is essentially untroubled by pests or disease, including deer and rabbits, and requires only an occasional light shearing after bloom to keep the mound tidy. Established clumps rarely need dividing and can be left undisturbed for many years.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Avondale Blue Wood Aster (Compact Lavender-Blue Heart-Leaved Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Avondale tolerates more shade than most garden asters.

directions: A selection of the native heart-leaved or blue wood aster, Avondale produces an unusually dense, self-branching mass of small lavender-blue flowers with contrasting darker centers, so floriferous that the foliage nearly disappears under bloom in late September and October. Its compact, well-branched habit and tolerance of light shade under trees set it apart from taller, more open woodland asters that tend to sprawl. It is a valuable very-late-season nectar source for bees and migrating butterflies when few other perennials are still flowering, and it self-sows modestly in favorable sites. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain a tidy, vigorous habit.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Goldenmosa is a garden hybrid and spreads far less aggressively than wild goldenrod species.

directions: Goldenmosa produces dense, fluffy, mimosa-like plumes of bright golden-yellow in late summer on a well-behaved, upright clump that stays far more restrained than the running native species it descends from. Its compact size and slower spread make it an easier fit for a mixed perennial border than most straight goldenrod species, without giving up the value to bees, small butterflies, and other late-season pollinators. It tolerates lean or average soil and dry spells with ease once established and holds its color well without fading in late-summer heat. Cut plants back hard in late fall or early spring and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to keep the planting vigorous and well shaped.
